what: Hlothhere and Eadric 16: a Kentishman who buys in Lundenwic has two or three true men as witnesses, or the king's wic-reeve; he vouches his seller at the king's hall in the town.
means: At lundenwic every purchase is made before the reeve or two witnesses. A thing bought without them can be claimed as stolen.
source: Laws of Hlothhere and Eadric 16 (Thorpe 1840, in Thatcher 1901); read on the Fordham sourcebook 6 Oct 2026

what: Hlothhere and Eadric 15: who keeps a stranger (a trader or another come over the border) three nights in his own home and feeds him answers for the harm he does.
means: Three nights lodged make a host: one sure oath-helper in that port, and the host answers for you. The act 'lodge'.
source: Laws of Hlothhere and Eadric 15 (from memory of Liebermann; not checked today)

what: Ine 11: who sells his own countryman over the sea, slave or free, pays his own wergild.
means: No English slave may be bought for export in Wessex: the seller's price is 200 shillings.
source: Laws of Ine 11 (from memory; in Design/content/economy/furs_amber_ivory_slaves.md)

what: Ine 20, Wihtred 28: a man from afar or a stranger who leaves the road and neither shouts nor blows a horn is taken for a thief, to be killed or ransomed.
means: A crewman sent inland keeps to the road or blows the horn. A small card ashore.
source: Laws of Ine 20; Wihtred 28 (from memory)

what: Ine 25: a trader who buys up-country does it before witnesses; if stolen goods are found with him he swears clear or pays 36 shillings.
means: Buying at villages and beaches needs witnesses, or the goods can be claimed.
source: Laws of Ine 25 (from memory)

what: Ine 23: a foreigner killed without kin: the king takes his wergild, or two thirds of it (?).
means: A stranger's protector is the king. A dead crewman's price goes to the king, not to the ship.
source: Laws of Ine 23 (from memory) (?)

where: Mercia and Kent: London, Fordwich, Sarre
what: The kings free one or two ships of a church from toll at London (Rochester, the bishops of London and Worcester, Minster in Thanet) and at Fordwich and Sarre (733 to c. 765). If the ship is lost, the freedom passes to her successor.
means: A toll existed at lundenwic, fordwic and sarre in 793; its rate is unknown. A church's ship goes free: carrying for a minster is toll-free.
source: Sawyer 86-88, 91, 98, 29 (from memory; numbers of ships (?))

what: Soissons c. 6: every town has a lawful market and lawful measures.
means: A Frankish town market is the king's and its measures are public.
source: MGH Capit. I no. 12 c. 6 (from memory)

what: Pippin confirms to St Martin's at Utrecht a tenth of the royal income in the land: estates, tolls and trade. Confirmed 769 and 815.
means: At dorestad and traiectum the bishop's man has a tenth of the king's tenth. Carrying for St Martin's makes friends at the toll house.
source: MGH DD Kar. 1 nos. 4, 5, 56 (from memory) (?)

what: Pippin's judgment gives all the tolls of the October fair of Saint-Denis to the abbey; the king's officers had taken four pennies a head from the merchants. Saxons (English) and Frisians come to it (?).
means: At parisius in October the toll is the abbey's, not the count's. A fair for wine and honey.
source: MGH DD Kar. 1 no. 6 (from memory) (?)

what: Pippin: no toll is taken from pilgrims at the passes, bridges and ferries.
means: A pilgrim passenger aboard is toll-free for his own things. Traders hide behind this (see 796).
source: MGH Capit. I no. 13 c. 4 (from memory)

what: A Frisian merchant kills a count's son at York; all the Frisians leave the city in fear, Liudger with them.
means: One countryman's crime shuts a port to his whole people for a season. At eoforwic a Frisian is watched.
source: Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.11-12 (from memory)

what: 8 June: Charlemagne gives St Martin's of Utrecht the church Upkirika at Dorestad and the bank toll (ripaticum) on the Lek.
means: A toll for lying at the bank at dorestad from before the game begins.
source: MGH DD Kar. 1 no. 117; nl.wikipedia Dorestad (the ripaticum and the year read 6 Oct 2026)

what: Herstal c. 18: no toll is taken except where it was of old.
means: A new toll is unlawful. A player who knows the law may refuse it.
source: MGH Capit. I no. 20 c. 18; en.wikipedia Capitulary of Herstal (outline read 6 Oct 2026; chapter numbers from memory)

what: Herstal c. 19: slaves are sold before the bishop, the count or their men, or good witnesses; nobody sells a slave beyond the march.
means: From 779 no slave is exported from the Frankish realm; a sale needs an officer present.
source: MGH Capit. I no. 20 c. 19; en.wikipedia Capitulary of Herstal

what: Herstal c. 20: nobody sells a mail coat out of the realm.
means: Byrnies may not be exported (trade_rules.json: arms, from 779).
source: MGH Capit. I no. 20 c. 20; en.wikipedia Capitulary of Herstal

what: Herstal c. 16: no sworn guilds; men may agree to help each other in alms, fire and shipwreck, but may not swear to it.
means: A wreck club among Dorestad's skippers is lawful as a promise. A 'work' to fund.
source: MGH Capit. I no. 20 c. 16 (from memory)

what: Herstal c. 10: a perjurer loses his hand.
means: A false oath at the toll house is a grave risk, not a small lie.
source: MGH Capit. I no. 20 c. 10 (from memory)

where: Francia: Rouen, Quentovic, Amiens, Maastricht, Dorestad
what: Charlemagne frees the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés from toll at these five places.
means: The five great toll stations of the north in one list. Cargo carried under the abbey's letter is free at rotomagus, quentovic and dorestad.
source: en.wikipedia Quentovic (read 6 Oct 2026); MGH DD Kar. 1 no. 122 (?)

what: Abbot Gervold of Saint-Wandrille is the king's procurator of trade to 806, collecting the tolls in the ports, above all at Quentovic. The royal toll there is a tenth.
means: At quentovic the chief toll officer is an abbot and Offa's friend: a real person to meet, 793 to 806.
source: Gesta abbatum Fontanellensium 12; en.wikipedia Quentovic (read 6 Oct 2026)

what: Admonitio generalis c. 74: equal measures and just weights in towns and monasteries, for giving and for taking.
means: False measure is the count's business. The acts 'weigh_silver' and 'sample' have law behind them.
source: MGH Capit. I no. 22 c. 74 (from memory)

what: Admonitio generalis c. 5: no usury for anybody.
means: The player's debt carries no interest: a fixed sum due on a day.
source: MGH Capit. I no. 22 c. 5 (from memory)

what: Charlemagne, angry over the marriage talks with Offa, forbids anybody from Britain to land in Gaul to trade. Ships are stopped on both sides until about 791.
means: The Channel is shut: no trade between Frankish and English ports for a Frankish subject. Lifted by 793; a memory the reeves still act on.
source: Gesta abbatum Fontanellensium 12; Alcuin's letter of 790; en.wikipedia Offa of Mercia (read 6 Oct 2026)

what: The custom of the strand: what the sea throws up belongs to the lord of the shore, and men thrown up with it may be seized. No king's law of the age forbids it; the Church does so only in 1179.
means: A wreck costs ship and cargo, and on a strange shore the crew may be held for ransom.
source: de.wikipedia Strandrecht (read 6 Oct 2026); no text of the period

where: The North: Norse and Svea trading places
what: The law of the trading place (later written as Bjarkeyjarréttr, 12th to 14th century): its own peace in the season, the king's man keeps it, crews settle disputes on the spot; it holds at every fishing station, herring ground and on trading voyages. No text from before 1100 survives.
means: Inside a northern market in the season there is a peace; a suit is heard the same day by the crews present; the king's man expects a gift.
source: en.wikipedia Bjarkey laws (read 6 Oct 2026); the Nidaros Bjarkeyjarréttr (from memory) (?)

what: The guest's due: fire, food and dry clothes for the man come in from the cold.
means: Hospitality is custom, not law, in the North; it is still owed.
source: Hávamál 3 (Bellows 1923), in texts_793.json

what: Frankfurt c. 4: grain not dearer than oats 1 d, barley 2 d, rye 3 d, wheat 4 d the public bushel; twelve wheat loaves of two pounds for a penny.
means: A lawful ceiling on grain and bread prices in the Frankish zone, even in a dear year.
source: MGH Capit. I no. 28 c. 4 (from memory)

what: Frankfurt c. 5: the new heavy pennies are taken everywhere; a free man who refuses them pays 15 solidi.
means: Nobody in Francia may refuse the king's new denier.
source: MGH Capit. I no. 28 c. 5 (from memory); Design/content/economy/silver_coin.md

what: Charlemagne to Offa: pilgrims go in peace, but those found trading among them pay toll; each king protects the other's merchants, who may appeal to him if wronged; black stones for England, and cloaks of the old length for Francia.
means: From 796 a wronged merchant in England or Francia may appeal to the king (the acts 'audience' and 'lawsuit'). A pilgrim's cloak does not free a cargo from toll.
source: Alcuin, Epistolae no. 100 (MGH Epp. IV); en.wikipedia Offa of Mercia (read 6 Oct 2026); chronicle 796-spring-offa-letter

what: Capitulare Saxonicum c. 11: a solidus in kind is a yearling ox, or 40 bushels of oats or 20 of rye (30 and 15 in the north); in silver twelve pennies.
means: In Saxony fines and prices are reckoned in cattle and grain: an ox is 12 d.
source: MGH Capit. I no. 27 c. 11 (from memory); chronicle 797-10-28-capitulare-saxonicum

what: Lex Frisionum I: wergilds of middle Frisia: a noble 80 solidi, a free man 53 solidi and a penny, a litus 27 less a penny to his lord and 9 to his kin; a slave at his worth. Women as men.
means: The price of a Frisian life, the player's own and his crew's. A free man is of the order of the starting debt (?).
source: Lex Frisionum I, XV (from memory; sums (?)); en. and de.wikipedia Lex Frisionum for date, ranks and lands (read 6 Oct 2026)

what: Lex Frisionum I: an accused man clears himself by oath with eleven helpers of his own rank; more if he is of lower rank than the man he wronged.
means: A suit at home is won by twelve men swearing. The odds are the count of your friends.
source: Lex Frisionum I (from memory)

what: Lex Frisionum XIV: a man killed in a crowd: up to seven are named, each swears with eleven, then lots are drawn on the altar or on relics, two sticks, one marked with a cross.
means: A killing on a crowded quay is settled by lot in the church. A card at dorestad or any Frisian port.
source: Lex Frisionum XIV (from memory)

what: Lex Frisionum III: a man accused of theft with no helpers goes to the boiling water: a stone from the kettle, the hand bound, looked at on the third day.
means: The ordeal for a friendless man accused of theft or of selling stolen goods.
source: Lex Frisionum III; en.wikipedia Lex Frisionum (the kettle read 6 Oct 2026)

what: Lex Frisionum XVII: who sells a slave to heathen peoples pays his own wergild to the king (?). XXI: who sells a free man out of the country pays as if he had killed him.
means: A Frisian who sells captives to Danes or Wends risks his own wergild from 802.
source: Lex Frisionum XVII.5, XXI (from memory) (?)

what: Lex Frisionum XVIII: no work on Sunday; a free man pays 12 solidi beyond the Lauwers and 4 elsewhere (?).
means: No loading or unloading on Sunday in Frisian ports.
source: Lex Frisionum XVIII (from memory) (?)

what: Additio sapientum XI: who breaks into a shrine and takes holy things is led to the sea and, on the sand the tide covers, his ears are slit, he is gelded and he is offered to the gods whose temple he dishonoured.
means: Heathen shrines on the Frisian coast are not to be robbed, even in a Christian king's law. An easter egg and a warning.
source: Lex Frisionum, Additio sapientum XI (from memory)

what: Lex Frisionum V: no wergild for a hired champion, a man killed in battle, an adulterer, a thief caught digging under a house, a man caught with a torch at a house, a shrine-breaker.
means: A thief or fire-raiser caught in the act on the ship may be killed without payment in Frisia.
source: Lex Frisionum V (from memory)

what: Lex Ribuaria 40 (36): a foreign Frank killed is 200 solidi; a foreign Alaman, Frisian, Bavarian or Saxon 160; a Roman 100. A wergild may be paid in kind: an ox 2 solidi, a cow 1, a sword with scabbard 7, a mail coat 12.
means: At colonia a Frisian's life is worth four fifths of a Frank's. Fines can be paid in goods at set values.
source: Lex Ribuaria 40 (36) (from memory; Design/economy_and_trade.md 1.2)

what: Ewa ad Amorem: a Frank 600 solidi, a free man 200, a litus 100, a slave 50.
means: The law at daventre.
source: Lex Francorum Chamavorum (from memory)

what: Capitulare missorum generale c. 27: nobody denies a roof, a fire and water to a pilgrim or a traveller.
means: Shelter cannot lawfully be refused in the Frankish realm. Food can.
source: MGH Capit. I no. 33 c. 27 (from memory); chronicle 802-10-aachen-laws-802

what: Arm-rings and mail coats are not given to merchants.
means: A merchant found with a byrnie in the hold must explain it.
source: MGH Capit. I no. 40 c. 7 (from memory) (?)

where: Francia's eastern border: Bardowick, Schezla, Magdeburg, Erfurt, Hallstadt, Forchheim, Premberg, Regensburg, Lorch
what: Thionville c. 7: merchants going to the Slavs and Avars go no farther than these nine places, each under a named officer, and carry no arms or mail to sell; if they do, all they carry is forfeit, half to the palace, half to the officers and the finder.
means: Arms may not go east. A searcher earns by finding: expect to be searched.
source: MGH Capit. I no. 44 c. 7; de.wikipedia Diedenhofener Kapitular (the date, the places and the ban read 6 Oct 2026); chronicle 805-12-thionville-arms

what: Thionville c. 13: old and just tolls are taken at bridges, ferries and markets; not where a rope is stretched or a ship passes under a bridge with no help given; and not from men carrying their own goods to their house, the palace or the army without meaning to trade.
means: Toll is on goods for sale. A player may declare 'my own goods' on his oath. New tolls may be refused.
source: MGH Capit. I no. 44 c. 13 (from memory); chronicle 805-12-thionville-tolls

what: Thionville c. 4: in a famine nobody sells food out of the empire.
means: A famine in Francia closes the export of grain and food.
source: MGH Capit. I no. 44 c. 4 (from memory); chronicle 805-12-thionville-famine

what: Thionville c. 5: nobody carries arms within the land: shield, lance, mail coat.
means: A crew goes unarmed ashore in Frankish ports.
source: MGH Capit. I no. 44 c. 5 (from memory)

what: Nobody trades at night in gold or silver vessels, slaves, gems, horses or beasts, except food and fodder for travellers; by day, before everybody and before witnesses.
means: At night a Frankish market sells only food and fodder.
source: MGH Capit. I no. 55 c. 2 (from memory; number and year (?))

what: Nijmegen cc. 11-17: usury is where more is asked back than was given; foul gain is buying grain or wine at harvest to sell dear later; honest trade is buying what one needs and selling the rest.
means: Holding wine or grain over a winter for the price is 'foul gain' in a churchman's eyes: a priest may say so. Not punished in a merchant.
source: MGH Capit. I no. 46 (from memory)

what: The best double cloak not dearer than 20 solidi, a single 10; a coat of marten or otter 30. Breakers pay 40 solidi, 20 of it to the informer.
means: A lawful ceiling on cloak and fur prices; an informer profits.
source: MGH Capit. I no. 52 c. 5 (from memory); Design/content/economy/cloth_wool.md

what: Godfred destroys Reric, which paid him great taxes, and moves its merchants to Sliesthorp.
means: The Danish king takes a due from trade at reric (to 808) and sliesthorp (after): the weighed-silver zone is not toll-free.
source: Royal Frankish Annals 808 (from memory); chronicle 808-summer-reric-destroyed

what: No toll where there is no bridge or ferry to help; no markets on Sunday except where they are of old.
means: Frankish markets are shut on Sunday, but for the old fairs.
source: MGH Capit. I nos. 61-62 (from memory) (?); chronicle 809-sunday-markets

what: Peace sworn on the river by twelve men of each side, Franks and Danes.
means: The Danish border is open to trade by treaty.
source: Royal Frankish Annals 811 (from memory); chronicle 811-spring-eider-peace

what: Louis the Pious forbids the ordeal of the cross; in 829 the ordeal of cold water.
means: After 829 the lawful ordeals in Francia are the kettle, the iron, the lots and the duel.
source: MGH Capit. I no. 138 c. 27; II no. 192 c. 12 (from memory)

what: Louis the Pious's letters for Jewish merchants (Donatus and Samuel; David and Joseph of Lyon; Abraham of Saragossa): they may buy foreign slaves and sell them within the empire; nobody baptises their slaves away from them.
means: The lawful slave road runs inside the empire, in the hands of the emperor's protected merchants.
source: Formulae imperiales 30, 31, 52 (from memory)

where: Francia: all the realm; Quentovic, Dorestad, the Clusae
what: The merchants' privilege: under the emperor's protection; to the palace each year or every second in mid May, serving the chamber; ships not seized for service; no toll anywhere except at Quentovic, Dorestad and the Clusae, where the tenth is taken; suits may wait for the emperor or the master set over the merchants.
means: The game's great charter from 828: toll-free everywhere in Francia but the tenth at dorestad and quentovic; a suit can be moved to the king. Cost: a May journey to the palace, gifts, and the chamber's commissions first. Renewed by each heir.
source: Formulae imperiales 37, MGH Formulae (Zeumer 1886) (from memory; not checked today)

what: The king cannot grant leave to preach on his own word: every public matter lies with the people's will. Lots are cast and the assembly decides, then a second assembly elsewhere. Hergeir is the king's officer of the place.
means: At birka a foreigner's request waits for the assembly and the lots: days, not silver. The king's man is the one to know.
source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii 11, 19, 26-27 (from memory; Robinson 1921); chronicle 829-ansgar-birka

what: Louis the Pious frees the men of the church of Strasbourg from toll through the realm, except at Quentovic, Dorestad and the Clusae.
means: Confirms the three places of the tenth. A Strasbourg cargo down the Rhine is free until dorestad.
source: Böhmer-Mühlbacher 890 (from memory)

what: Louis the Pious gives the abbey of Corvey a mint, because the region lacked a place of trade.
means: From 833 coin is struck inland on the Weser; markets and mints begin to be given to churches.
source: Böhmer-Mühlbacher 922 (from memory)

where: Venice and the kingdom of Italy
what: Pactum Lotharii: no Christian is bought or sold; fugitives are returned.
means: The southern slave road is closed to Christian captives by treaty.
source: Pactum Lotharii (from memory)

what: Rorik the Dane takes Dorestad and Lothar accepts him as his man to hold it against other Danes.
means: From 850 the tenth at dorestad is taken by a Dane's men. The emperor's charters may not be honoured there.
source: Annals of St-Bertin and of Fulda 850 (from memory); chronicle 850-rorik-dorestad

what: Horik the elder allows a church at the port; afterwards merchants from Dorestad, Hamburg and Bremen go there freely and without fear.
means: From about 850 a Christian merchant is safe at sliesthorp under the king's word.
source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii 24 (from memory)

what: Burgred of Mercia grants the bishop of Worcester a plot by the west gate with free use of the scale, the weights and the measures of the port.
means: Weighing at London is a royal right; a house of one's own there with its own scale is a 'work' worth having.
source: Sawyer 208 (from memory)

where: West Francia (Charles the Bald's kingdom): Quentovic, Rouen, Paris, the Seine and Loire
what: Pîtres c. 25: whoever gives a mail coat, weapons or a horse to the Northmen, for any reason or any ransom, loses his life as a traitor.
means: No arms or horses to Northmen from West Frankish ports, not even as ransom. Not law at dorestad or on the Rhine.
source: MGH Capit. II no. 273 c. 25; en. and fr.wikipedia on the edict (read 6 Oct 2026); chronicle 864-06-25-pitres

what: Pîtres cc. 8-18: new pennies of 1.75 g from ten mints (the palace, Quentovic, Rouen, Reims, Sens, Paris, Orléans, Chalon, Melle, Narbonne); after Martinmas only the new are taken; who refuses a good penny is fined or flogged.
means: Old coin dies at Martinmas 864 in the west; change it at quentovic, rotomagus or parisius.
source: MGH Capit. II no. 273; fr.wikipedia Édit de Pîtres (read 6 Oct 2026); the mint list from memory; Design/content/economy/silver_coin.md

what: Pîtres c. 19: each count lists the markets of his county, old and new, and by whose leave; the king decides which stay.
means: A new or unlicensed market can be shut by the count.
source: MGH Capit. II no. 273 c. 19 (from memory)

what: Pîtres cc. 20, 23-24: measures true to the palace's, the cheat fined or flogged; gold and silver sold pure; a pound of gold for twelve of silver.
means: False measure has a penalty; the gold rate is 12 to 1.
source: MGH Capit. II no. 273; fr.wikipedia Édit de Pîtres (the 12 : 1 and the penalties for mixed metal read 6 Oct 2026)

what: No king's measure: each merchant carries folding scales and weights to a common standard (the ertog about 8 g, the øre about 25 g, the mark about 200 g); silver is nicked to test it.
means: In the weighed-silver lands both sides weigh. A set of true weights is a thing to own.
source: Finds at Birka, Hedeby and Kaupang (from memory); Design/content/economy/silver_coin.md

where: The Eider: Danes and East Franks
what: King Sigifrid's men ask Louis the German for peace on the border so that merchants of either realm may come and go and buy and sell in peace. Granted.
means: The road between sliesthorp and Saxony is open to merchants by treaty.
source: Annals of Fulda 873 (from memory)

what: The Danish army swears peace to Alfred on the holy ring, which it would not do before for any people; and breaks it.
means: A Dane's great oath is on the ring, a Christian's on relics. An oath across faiths is sworn twice.
source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 876 (from memory)

where: England and the Danish east (between 878 and 890)
what: Alfred and Guthrum: the border up the Thames, the Lea, to Bedford and up the Ouse to Watling Street; a man of either people is paid for with eight half-marks of gold; a king's thegn clears himself with twelve king's thegns.
means: The Danelaw's border on the chart. One price for Dane and Englishman.
source: en.wikipedia Treaty of Alfred and Guthrum (read 6 Oct 2026)

where: England and the Danish east (between 878 and 890)
what: Alfred and Guthrum 4-5: every man knows his warrantor when he buys slaves, horses or oxen; nobody crosses to the other side without leave, but trade is allowed when hostages are given as a pledge of peace.
means: Crossing the line to trade costs a hostage or a bond; slaves, horses and oxen need a named seller.
source: en.wikipedia Treaty of Alfred and Guthrum (read 6 Oct 2026)

what: King Arnulf gives Archbishop Rimbert market, mint and toll at Bremen.
means: Bremen becomes a toll market under the archbishop.
source: MGH DD Arn. 27 (from memory)

what: Alfred and Æthelred grant the bishop of Worcester a plot at Hwætmund's stone: sales inside the yard pay toll to the bishop; sales in the street or on the trading shore pay to the king.
means: At London after 886 toll is the king's on the strand and a lord's inside his own yard.
source: Sawyer 346 (from memory)

what: Alfred 34: traders bring the men they take up-country before the king's reeve at the folk-moot and say how many; they take only men they can bring to justice.
means: The skipper answers for his crew ashore in Wessex and shows them to the reeve.
source: Laws of Alfred 34 (from memory)

what: King Zwentibold confirms Utrecht's rights; the toll once taken at Dorestad is taken at Tiel.
means: From 896 the Rhine toll is at Tiel, not dorestad.
source: en.wikipedia Tiel (the toll right of 896 read 6 Oct 2026); the wording (?)

what: Landaurar: every ship sailing from Norway to Iceland owes the king a fee, set by Harald Finehair at five ounces (?).
means: A landing fee in Norway on the Iceland trade.
source: Ari, Íslendingabók 1 (from memory) (?)

where: The Danube: Raffelstetten, Rosdorf, Linz, Mautern (903 to 906)
what: The toll inquest under Margrave Aribo: a ship from the west pays half a drachma at Rosdorf; three bushels of salt at Linz; slaves and other goods then free as far as the Bohemian forest; Slavs pay in wax by the load; a solidus a ship at the Moravians' market; Jews and other merchants pay the old just toll.
means: The model of a river toll: fixed sums by the ship and the load, in coin or in the cargo itself, set by what the old men swear was custom.
source: MGH Capit. II no. 253; en. and de.wikipedia on the Raffelstetten regulations (read 6 Oct 2026)

what: On a slave woman one tremissa, the same on a stallion; on a male slave one saiga, the same on a mare (?).
means: Slaves and horses pay toll by the head, not by value.
source: MGH Capit. II no. 253 (from memory) (?); Design/content/economy/furs_amber_ivory_slaves.md

what: The treaty: the Rus lodge at St Mamas, are listed, enter by one gate unarmed, fifty at a time; six months' keep; no toll; a ship cast ashore is helped and brought to safety by the other side.
means: The Rus pay no toll at byzantium by treaty; wreck is not plunder between the two peoples.
source: Russian Primary Chronicle, 907 and 911 (from memory); chronicle 911-09-02-rus-treaty

what: I Edward 1: no man buys outside a port; he has the port-reeve's witness or that of other truthful men.
means: English trade is drawn into the ports under the reeve's eye.
source: I Edward 1 (Thorpe 1840, in Thatcher 1901); read on the Fordham sourcebook 6 Oct 2026

what: The king of the Bulghars takes one slave in ten from every Rus ship. Earlier (c. 850) the Rus pay a tenth to the emperor and a tenth to the Khazar king.
means: The tenth on the Volga road (trade_rules.json, the dirham zone) is sourced.
source: Ibn Fadlan; Ibn Khurradadhbih (from memory)

what: The synod: who sells a Christian is guilty of his killing.
means: Selling a Christian is a killing in the Church's law.
source: Synod of Koblenz 922 c. 7 (from memory; in Design/economy_and_trade.md)

what: II Athelstan 12: no man buys anything over twenty pence outside a port; inside, on the witness of the port-reeve.
means: From c. 928 a beach or village deal over 20 pence is unlawful in England.
source: II Athelstan 12 (Thorpe 1840, in Thatcher 1901); read on the Fordham sourcebook 6 Oct 2026; chronicle 928-grately-laws

what: II Athelstan 14: one money over all the king's realm, minted only in a port; moneyers by town (London 8, Canterbury 7, Winchester 6, Rochester 3, Hamwic 2 and others); a false moneyer loses his hand.
means: Coin is changed only in the named ports.
source: II Athelstan 14 (quote read on Fordham 6 Oct 2026; the list from memory)

what: II Athelstan 18: nobody sends a horse over the sea, unless as a gift.
means: Horses may not be exported from England from c. 928.
source: II Athelstan 18 (from memory)

what: The ordeal: three days with the priest on bread, water, salt and herbs; the iron of one pound (three for the threefold) carried nine feet, or the hand in the kettle to the wrist (the elbow for the threefold); bound and looked at on the third day.
means: The ordeal costs three days before and three after, whatever the end.
source: II Athelstan 23 and the ordeal dooms (weights and third day read on Fordham 6 Oct 2026; nine feet from memory)

what: VI Athelstan: the peace-guild of London: four pence a year; stolen goods paid for at a horse half a pound, an ox a mancus, a cow 20 d, a pig 10 d, a sheep a shilling, a slave half a pound.
means: A guild that insures against theft, and a sourced price list for England about 935.
source: VI Athelstan 6 (from memory)

what: The treaty: the Rus bring their prince's charter saying how many ships; no silk above 50 gold pieces a man, sealed by the officer.
means: A limit on silk bought at byzantium, and a charter needed to trade there.
source: Russian Primary Chronicle 944 (from memory); chronicle 944-igor-treaty

what: III Edgar 8: one coinage; one measure and one weight as kept at London and Winchester; the wey of wool at 120 pence and not cheaper.
means: One standard of weight in England, and a floor price for wool.
source: III Edgar 8 (from memory); Design/content/economy/cloth_wool.md

what: IV Edgar 3-11: sworn witnesses, thirty-six in each borough, twelve in a small borough or hundred; every sale before two or three of them.
means: From c. 962 an English sale has sworn witnesses by office.
source: IV Edgar (from memory)

what: The priest Poppo carries the glowing iron unhurt before Harald Bluetooth; the king is baptised.
means: After c. 965 the Danes know and trust the ordeal of the iron.
source: Widukind III.65 (from memory)

what: Otto I gives the archbishops market, mint and toll; the merchants of Bremen are under the king's protection with the rights of merchants in the other royal towns.
means: A merchant settled in a royal market town has the king's protection by that alone.
source: MGH DD O I 300, 307 (from memory)

where: The German kingdom: Mainz, Cologne, Tiel, Bardowick
what: Otto II frees the merchants of Magdeburg from toll everywhere except at Mainz, Cologne, Tiel and Bardowick.
means: The four great toll places of the 10th-century kingdom. Tiel has taken dorestad's place.
source: MGH DD O II 112 (from memory)

what: Máel Sechnaill takes Dublin and lays on it an ounce of gold from every garth, each Christmas night for ever.
means: At duiblinn after 989 the Irish over-king takes a yearly tax from the town.
source: Annals of Tigernach 989 (from memory) (?)

what: II Æthelred: every merchant ship that comes into a river mouth has peace; if she is driven ashore and the men reach a borough with what they carry, they and it have peace; a free man of either side killed is 25 pounds, a slave one pound.
means: From 994 a merchant ship in English waters has the king's peace even from the fleet; a wreck near a borough saves what the crew can carry.
source: II Æthelred 2-5 (from memory)

what: III Æthelred (Wantage): the twelve leading thegns swear on relics to accuse no innocent man and hide no guilty one.
means: In the Danish east of England a charge comes from a sworn twelve.
source: III Æthelred 3.1 (from memory)

what: IV Æthelred 2: a small boat pays a halfpenny, a larger boat with a sail a penny, a keel or hulk four pence if she lies there; a ship with planks one plank; cloth pays toll on Sunday, Tuesday and Thursday.
means: From c. 1000 the toll at lundenwic is by the ship: the player's boat pays a halfpenny or a penny.
source: IV Æthelred 2 (Liebermann; from memory); earlyenglishlaws.ac.uk (outline read 6 Oct 2026); chronicle 1000-london-tolls

what: IV Æthelred 2: the men of Rouen with wine or blubber-fish pay six shillings for a great ship and a twentieth of the fish; the men of Flanders, Ponthieu, Normandy and Francia show their goods and pay toll; those of Huy, Liège and Nivelles pay for the showing and toll.
means: Each foreign people has its own terms at London. A Rouen wine ship pays 72 pence.
source: IV Æthelred 2 (from memory); earlyenglishlaws.ac.uk (outline)

what: IV Æthelred 2: the Emperor's men, who come in their own ships, are worthy of good laws as the English are; they may buy wool and melted fat and three live pigs for the ship, may not forestall the townsmen, and pay at Christmas and at Easter two grey cloths and one brown, ten pounds of pepper, five pairs of gloves and two kegs of vinegar.
means: A Tiel or Cologne house is 'the Emperor's men' at London: good law, wool, and a due in kind twice a year. A standing commission.
source: IV Æthelred 2 (from memory); earlyenglishlaws.ac.uk (outline); Design/content/economy/cloth_wool.md

what: IV Æthelred 5-9: merchants who bring false or light coin clear themselves or pay; every weight is stamped to the king's, fifteen ores to the pound.
means: Weights at London are the king's and stamped. Bad coin is the bringer's risk.
source: IV Æthelred 5-9 (from memory); Design/content/economy/silver_coin.md

what: V Æthelred 2: Christian men and innocent men are not sold out of the land, least of all to heathens. 24: false weights and wrongful measures are put away.
means: From 1008 no Christian slave may be exported from England.
source: V Æthelred 2, 24 (from memory); again in II Cnut 3, 9

what: The heregeld, the army-tax for the hired fleet, is paid yearly until Edward ends it in 1051.
means: A land tax, not a toll; it makes silver scarce in English markets (?).
source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 1012, 1051 (from memory)

what: Count Dirk III takes a toll of his own from the Tiel merchants bound for England; the emperor's army sent against him is beaten on 29 July.
means: A new and unlawful toll on the road from tiel to England that nobody can remove.
source: Alpert of Metz II.20-21; Thietmar VIII (from memory); chronicle 1018-07-29-vlaardingen

what: The merchants of Tiel judge by their own will and not by the law, say they have the emperor's charter for it, clear debts by oath, and drink together on feast days from a common fund.
means: The first merchants' law of their own. A house of Tiel can be judged by its fellows.
source: Alpert of Metz, De diversitate temporum II.20 (from memory); chronicle 1020-tiel-merchants

what: II Cnut 8-9, 24: one coinage; just weights and measures; nothing over four pence bought without four true witnesses, in borough or up-country.
means: Under Cnut any purchase over four pence needs four witnesses.
source: II Cnut 8, 9, 24 (from memory)

what: Olaf Haraldsson's law for the Icelanders: in Norway they have a hauldr's rights; they pay landaurar of six cloaks and six ells of homespun or half a mark of silver; nothing if storm-driven; wood and water free; they help defend the land.
means: A landing fee in Norwegian ports in goods or silver, waived for a ship driven in by weather.
source: The Icelanders' rights in Norway, in Grágás (from memory)

what: Cnut gives Christ Church, Canterbury, the port of Sandwich and its tolls, as far inland as a small axe can be thrown from a ship afloat at high tide (?).
means: A port's toll can belong to a church, and its reach is measured from the ship.
source: Sawyer 959, of doubtful genuineness (from memory) (?)

what: Cnut's letter: the emperor Conrad, King Rudolf and the princes grant that his people, merchants and pilgrims, go to Rome and back free of the barriers and the toll-takers, in firm peace and under just law.
means: From 1027 English and Danish merchants pay no toll at the Clusae. Cnut's men have a king who bargains for them.
source: Cnut's letter of 1027 in William of Malmesbury and John of Worcester (from memory); en.wikipedia Cnut (read 6 Oct 2026); chronicle 1027-03-26-cnut-rome

what: A ship coming or going without the king's leave: 40 shillings a man; one coming against the king's peace is forfeit, ship, men and goods; with leave, four pence a load on leaving; the reeve has first purchase of marten skins; false measure four shillings.
means: At legacaestir ask leave before landing; furs go past the reeve first.
source: Domesday Book, Cheshire (from memory)

what: The seller of a horse gives the reeve a penny and the buyer another; of an ox a halfpenny; of a man four pence.
means: A market toll by the head on beasts and slaves.
source: Domesday Book, Sussex (from memory; in Design/content/economy/furs_amber_ivory_slaves.md)

what: The burgesses give the king twenty ships for fifteen days a year and are quit of toll through all England.
means: At dofras ship service buys freedom from toll.
source: Domesday Book, Kent (from memory)

what: Bishop Wulfstan of Worcester preaches the Bristol men out of selling English slaves to Ireland (c. 1060 to 1090).
means: The Irish Sea slave trade from England ends by preaching, not by law.
source: William of Malmesbury, Vita Wulfstani II.20 (from memory)

where: The Baltic: Sambia; the North Sea: Heligoland
what: Adam of Bremen: the Sembi go out to help those in peril on the sea or attacked by pirates; on Heligoland no raider dares take anything.
means: A wreck on the Sembian coast is helped. Heligoland is a safe and holy place: take nothing from it.
source: Adam of Bremen IV.3, IV.18 (from memory), written c. 1075
